sections.content: You know *tú* and *usted* from A1, *señor* and *señora* from A1 Unit 1, and *usted* commands from A2 Unit 23. This lesson is about choosing between *tú* and *usted*, about *don* and *doña*, and about recognising *vos*, a third word for "you".

sections.title: Choosing between tú and usted
sections.content: *Tú* is for people you are close to: family, friends, classmates, children. *Usted* shows respect or distance: strangers, older people, customers, someone senior at work. *Usted* takes the same verb form as *él* and *ella*. The line moves from place to place: in parts of Colombia and in Costa Rica, people also use *usted* with family and close friends. Usually the older person, or the one with more authority, is the one who offers *tú*.

In Spain, *tú* is used more widely than in most of Latin America: often with colleagues, shop staff and people of your own age. The plural is different too. In Spain, *vosotros* is the plural of *tú* (*¿Venís a la fiesta?*, to two friends) and *ustedes* the plural of *usted* (*¿Vienen ustedes?*, to two clients). In Latin America, *ustedes* is the only plural, for friends and strangers alike.

sections.title: Ways to address someone
rows: Buenos días, don Manuel. ¿Cómo está usted?
Good morning, Don Manuel. How are you? (respect: *don* + first name)
Shall we use *tú* with each other?

sections.title: Don, doña, señor, señora
sections.content: *Don* and *doña* go before a first name: *don Manuel*, *doña Rosa*. They show respect for an older or well-regarded person and sound warmer than *señor* and *señora*, which go with a surname or stand alone. Never use *don* with a surname.

sections.title: Recognising vos (Argentina and Uruguay)
sections.content:
In Argentina and Uruguay, people say *vos* where other countries say *tú*. You do not need to use it. You need to recognise it when you hear it or meet it in a film or a book.

In the present, *vos* takes the infinitive, drops the final *-r* and stresses the last syllable: *hablar → vos hablás*, *comer → vos comés*, *vivir → vos vivís*. Stem changes disappear: *tú quieres* but *vos querés*, *tú puedes* but *vos podés*. So *tú tienes* becomes *vos tenés*. The one irregular form is *ser*: *tú eres → vos sos*. The command also drops the *-r*: *vení* (come), *mirá* (look), *decime* (tell me). *Te* and *tu* stay the same.

sections.title: Vos and tú side by side
rows: Vos sabés la respuesta. / Tú sabes la respuesta.
Vos tenés razón. / Tú tienes razón.
Vos sos muy amable. / Tú eres muy amable.
Vení a casa. / Ven a casa.
Decime la verdad. / Dime la verdad.

sections.content: With *vos*, the verb form is the clue: *-ás*, *-és*, *-ís* at the end, or *sos*. If you hear *vos podés* in Montevideo, think "you can" and answer in your own *tú* or *usted*; nobody expects a visitor to switch.
